text:
The European Commission is drawing flak for offering fiscal leeway to contend with skyrocketing fuel prices.

AI generated Text-to-speech

LUXEMBOURG — France has told Brussels it is “very concerned” about plans to exempt green investments from the EU’s public spending rules, two diplomats told POLITICO.

Paris joined Estonia, Finland and the Netherlands in blasting the European Commission’s new fiscal waiver to provide a cushion against rising energy costs when they met for a closed-door discussion of eurozone finance ministers in Luxembourg Thursday, said four diplomats at the meeting who were granted anonymity to discuss the topic.

Other countries urged “caution” over the EU executive’s exemption during the Eurogroup meeting, two of the diplomats said, after the bloc’s fiscal watchdog warned that bending the fiscal rules too much could imperil their credibility.

The Commission presented the waiver in early June to give some budgetary breathing space for countries contending with skyrocketing fuel prices due to the conflict in Iran.

EU treasuries will soon receive an explanatory note that outlines how the waiver will work in greater detail, Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis told reporters after the Eurogroup, while acknowledging countries’ concerns.

“The views on this topic were varying, but all in all, there was acknowledgment of the need to work toward reducing our dependency on fossil fuels,” the Latvian said.

The rise in energy prices has been particularly painful for heavily indebted countries such as Italy and France, which are already trying to rein in spending to align with the EU’s fiscal rules after a pause during the pandemic.

Paris, for example, has put €6 billion of its spending plans for this year on hold in response to the energy crisis. Regardless, the concession has not sat well with France, a country that has enjoyed fiscal flexibility from Brussels in the past.

France’s finance minister, Roland Lescure, wasn’t present at Thursday’s Eurogroup. But the representative attending in his place told the EU executive that Paris was “very concerned” over the waiver, the two diplomats said.

The Commission announced the fiscal concession following pressure from Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, who urged Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to extend an existing waiver for defense spending — amounting to 1.5 percent of GDP — to energy-related expenditures.

The Commission obliged, but only for investments into green initiatives that EU capitals have been pursuing since February, when the conflict in Iran began, to reduce their reliance on fossil fuels. Such initiatives include subsidies to help households and businesses change their heating systems “from gas or diesel to heat pumps” and “batteries to store energy from solar panels,” Dombrovskis said.

The waiver is limited to investments worth 0.6 percent of GDP over three years until 2028, allowing cash-strapped governments to free up extra budget space to support citizens and companies who face higher energy bills. (EU countries cannot spend more than 0.3 percent of GDP over a single year.) Governments will have to apply for the waiver, which will also need the support of a qualified majority within the Council.

Brussels’ rules for public spending are supposed to limit countries’ budget deficits to 3 percent of economic output, while debt levels are supposed to stay under 60 percent of GDP. But the reality is often a different story: Italy’s debt climbed above 137 percent of its GDP at the end of last year, second behind Greece at 146 percent. France is the EU’s third most indebted country at around 115 percent of its economic output.

Such levels of debt don’t leave much room for maneuver, as the International Monetary Fund’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, stressed after the Eurogroup.

“Please, please, please, for those who are with high deficit, high debt, be very careful not to spend money you don’t have,” she said.

CORRECTION: An earlier version of this report misquoted Valdis Dombrovskis. This article was updated June 12 to correct that he said the views were “varying.”

The campaign for influence comes as political momentum behind the EU’s decade-long bid to create a U.S.-style financial market gathers pace.

The European Commission is trying to figure out who provides the cash when a rescued lender needs to regain market trust.

The EU’s big six will now have to rally other governments to join their cause without making it look like they’re ignoring the views of contrarian countries.

Brussels is taking full advantage after the former prime minister’s election loss in Hungary last month.
